A company for which EODHD reports neither figure receives total_debt = 0.00, which reads as "this company has no debt" and is indistinguishable from a genuine debt-free balance sheet. This is the same class of defect as v11.2.74, where `if f != 0 else None` erased every disclosed zero -- here it runs the other way, manufacturing a disclosed zero from an absence. Any debt-free screen built on total_debt = 0 will include companies whose debt is merely unknown.

transformation_rule: The staging DATE is anchored to a fixed +10:00 offset at 16:00, the ASX close, producing 06:00 UTC.
business_rule: FIXED OFFSET, NOT A ZONE, AND DELIBERATELY SO. 'Australia/Sydney' is the tempting spelling and is wrong in principle: it shifts to +11 under daylight saving and the write does not. Reading back must use the exact inverse -- (time AT TIME ZONE INTERVAL '+10:00')::date -- or a row can be attributed to the wrong calendar day. The two spellings agree today only because 06:00 UTC falls on the same date at both offsets, which is agreement by luck.
UNADJUSTED. As traded on the day.
UNADJUSTED intraday high.
UNADJUSTED intraday low.

UNADJUSTED closing price, and NOT NULL -- the only price column that is. Every return and momentum measure in the product is computed on THIS column, not on adjusted_close. That choice is deliberate but it means a raw close series crosses splits and large capital returns without a discontinuity marker, so a return spanning a split is a price artefact unless the split is applied separately. See market.splits, which exists to supply that correction.

DO NOT USE FOR PRICE RETURNS. Two independent problems: it is a TOTAL-RETURN series (dividends reinvested), so it answers a different question from close; and it is not maintained in step with close, so it can be stale relative to the same row's close. Nullable, unlike close.
Shares traded, unadjusted for splits -- so a volume series crosses a split with a step change in the opposite direction to price.
ALWAYS NULL. Named by none of the eight writers. Dollar turnover would have to be derived (volume x vwap, or volume x close as a proxy) and nothing does so.
ALWAYS NULL. EODHD's end-of-day feed does not carry a trade count.
ALWAYS NULL. Volume-weighted average price requires intraday data the end-of-day feed does not provide.

THE COLUMN DEFAULT IS 'yahoo', WHICH NO CURRENT PATH USES. Any row written without naming this column carries a provenance that is false. With eight writers across three providers this is the only field that says which one produced a row, so a wrong default is not cosmetic.
Surrogate key. The business key is (asx_code, ex_date, dividend_type).
The EODHD dividend date IS the ex-date. This is the date the price drops by the dividend, and the date a yield calculation must align to -- not the payment date.
Typically one business day after ex_date. Often NULL in the source.

THE POPULATED ONE OF THE PAIR. Source staging_au.dividends.payment_date lands here, in market.dividends.pay_date. The similarly named market.dividends.payment_date column is NOT written by this transform -- see below. Reading payment_date on this table returns NULL while the value sits in pay_date.
Renamed from the source field. Often NULL.

transformation_rule: float(value); rows where it is NULL are SKIPPED
business_rule:
NOT NULL by constraint, enforced by dropping source rows with a NULL dividend before insert (transform_dividends.py:121-122). Those rows are counted and logged, not silently discarded, but they do not reach this table at all -- so a dividend EODHD announced without an amount is absent rather than present-and-unknown.
UNADJUSTED cash amount per share, in the currency of the `currency` column. Not restated for later splits, so a historical dividend is expressed per the share count of its own time and will not align with a split-adjusted price series.

transformation_rule: defaults to AUD when the source states none
business_rule: THE FALLBACK IS AN ASSUMPTION, NOT A FACT. A missing source currency becomes 'AUD'. Dual-listed and USD-reporting companies do pay non-AUD dividends, and for those a silent AUD default makes a grossed-up yield wrong by the exchange rate. Compare staging_au.fundamentals.reporting_currency, which deliberately keeps NULL distinct from AUD for the same reason.

Percentage of the dividend carrying franking credits, 0-100. THE COLUMN DEFAULT IS 0, so a row written without this column asserts "unfranked" rather than "unknown" -- a confident negative. Where the source supplies NULL the value is copied as NULL, which is the honest state; the default only bites on paths that omit the column.

ALWAYS NULL. Named by none of the three writers. The franking credit is computed downstream from amount_per_share and franking_pct at the company tax rate; this column was intended to persist it and does not.

ALWAYS NULL. Named by none of the three writers. Grossed-up yield -- the product's distinguishing metric -- is computed downstream rather than stored here. Anyone reading this column expecting the grossed-up figure gets NULL, not a wrong number, which is the better failure.

PART OF THE UNIQUE KEY, and nullable. Values come from EODHD's period label lowercased -- 'interim', 'final', and similar. When the source omits period the value is NULL, and NULLs do not collide in a UNIQUE constraint, so two unlabelled dividends on the same ex-date can both insert. The deduplication this key is supposed to provide does not hold for exactly the rows whose type is unknown.
derivation_formula: dividend_type = period.lower() if period else None

business_rule: ALWAYS false. No writer sets it. A confident negative: it asserts no dividend reinvestment plan exists, for every dividend ever paid, including the many that do have one.
ALWAYS NULL. No writer sets it.

THE EMPTY HALF OF A DUPLICATE PAIR. The payment date supplied by staging is written to pay_date, not here. Two columns for one fact, with the populated one named differently from the source field it came from. Code selecting payment_date gets NULL and has no signal that pay_date holds the answer.

NULL from this transform, although staging_au.dividends carries an unadjusted_value column. EODHD distinguishes the adjusted dividend (restated for later splits) from the unadjusted one; amount_per_share here receives the `dividend` field. Which of the two that is depends on EODHD's own convention and is not established by this mapping -- flagged as an open question rather than asserted.

THE EMPTY HALF OF THE SECOND DUPLICATE PAIR. dividend_type is the populated column and the one in the UNIQUE key; div_type is a wider varchar(50) that stays NULL. Two columns, one fact, and the one with the more natural name is the empty one.

transformation_rule: direct copy of the formatted period end
business_rule: THE PERIOD THE COUNT REFERS TO, not when it was observed. Part of the primary key. Pair with snapshot_date below, which is the other date and means something else entirely.
column_comment: Period end the share count refers to, from outstandingShares.annual dateFormatted. NOT the date the snapshot was taken.

business_rule: Share count at fiscal_date, unadjusted for later splits. A series crossing a split therefore steps, and the step is real rather than an error -- market.splits carries the ratio that reconciles it.

transformation_rule: direct copy of the source's own millions figure
business_rule: NOT DERIVED FROM `shares` -- both come from the provider. They can therefore disagree, and nothing constrains them to agree. Prefer `shares` as the authority; treat a mismatch as a source-quality signal rather than a rounding artefact.

PART OF THE PRIMARY KEY, which is what lets a second provider coexist rather than overwrite. Also means a consumer that forgets to filter on source will fan out one row per provider once a second one exists.

transformation_rule: direct copy of the fundamentals file date
business_rule: WHEN THE OBSERVATION WAS TAKEN, not what period it describes. Two snapshots can report different counts for the same fiscal_date after a restatement; the newest snapshot wins on upsert, so the prior reported count is overwritten and not recoverable from this table.
column_comment: Date of the fundamentals file supplying this row. Two snapshots can report different counts for the same fiscal_date after a restatement; the newest snapshot wins on upsert.

business_rule: Row write time. A third date, distinct from both above.

ASIC's own report date, NOT the date it was fetched. ASIC publishes with a 2-3 business day lag, so the newest row here is always several days behind the market. A short-interest figure presented beside a live price is comparing two different days.
Reported short positions as a percentage of total issued capital. ASIC's own figure, not recomputed from short_shares / total_issued.
Reported short position in shares. staging_au.short_positions also carries total_issued, which is NOT promoted to this table -- so the denominator behind short_pct is not available here.

transformation_rule: Difference against the previous ASIC snapshot, computed only for the most recent report_date in staging.
business_rule:
A DIFFERENCE IN PERCENTAGE POINTS, not a percentage change. A move from 2% to 3% short gives 1.0, not 50.
"1w" IS APPROXIMATE. The window is "the previous snapshot, if within 14 days" -- so over a holiday period or a publication gap the figure can span two weeks while still being labelled one. NULL when no prior snapshot exists inside 14 days, which is the honest outcome and must not be read as "no change".
join_condition: prior = the most recent report_date strictly BEFORE the current one and no more than 14 days earlier, same asx_code

transformation_rule: column default now(), refreshed on upsert
business_rule: When this row was last written. Says nothing about how current ASIC's data is -- report_date is the column that does.
The effective date of the split. Prices on and after this date are on the new share basis; prices before it are not.

transformation_rule:
parse_ratio() accepts both EODHD spellings:
  '2:1'                -> 2.0   (2-for-1 forward split)
  '1:10'               -> 0.1   (1-for-10 reverse split)
  '1.000000/5.000000'  -> 0.2   (1-for-5 reverse, slash form)
business_rule:
GREATER THAN 1 IS A FORWARD SPLIT, LESS THAN 1 IS A REVERSE SPLIT. To restate a pre-split price onto the current basis, DIVIDE by the ratio; to restate a share count, multiply. Getting this inverted turns a 1-for-40 consolidation into a 40x price move.
A ratio's MAGNITUDE must account for the price discontinuity it is offered to explain. A split record whose ratio is too small to explain an observed move does not explain it -- MPP's 1-for-40 silenced a detector while the price moved 1,564x, which is the reason that test exists.
NULL when the source string is absent or unparseable. A NULL ratio on a real split is worse than no row: the date says a discontinuity exists and the ratio cannot correct it.
derivation_formula: ratio = new_shares / old_shares, parsed from the source string

business_rule: Column default is also 'eodhd' here, so unlike market.daily_prices the default and the writer agree.
When this row was written, not when the split occurred. Not a lineage marker for the source.
